clinicalScope: Liver function tests in adult patients in low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Liver Function Tests
subject: Medicine
summary: Liver function tests (LFTs) are a panel of blood tests that assess liver health by measuring enzymes, proteins and bilirubin. In low‑resource settings they guide diagnosis of common tropical liver diseases and drug toxicity, but results must be interpreted with clinical context.

sections.p: LFTs are not a single test but a group of assays that reflect hepatocellular injury, cholestasis, synthetic function and haemolysis. They are usually ordered together as a ‘liver panel’.
b: GGT – biliary activity and drug exposure
Bilirubin (total, direct, indirect) – excretion of urobilinogen

t.b: ↑ indicates liver or muscle damage; >10× ULN suggests acute injury
↑ is more liver‑specific; >5× ULN suggests acute hepatitis
↑ with normal GGT suggests bone or pregnancy; ↑ with high GGT suggests biliary obstruction
↑ supports cholestasis or alcohol use; normal GGT with high ALP points to bone
↑ indicates impaired excretion or haemolysis; direct >20% suggests conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
↓ indicates chronic liver disease or protein loss
↑ indicates synthetic failure or vitamin K deficiency

sections.p: In East Africa the most frequent causes of abnormal LFTs are infectious, metabolic and iatrogenic.
b: Hepatitis B and C – endemic, often asymptomatic until cirrhosis
Malaria‑related hepatic injury – especially severe falciparum
Alcoholic liver disease – increasing with urbanisation
Non‑alcoholic fatty liver disease – linked to obesity, HIV
Drug‑induced liver injury – antituberculars, antimalarials, antiretrovirals

t.b: Positive indicates chronic infection; high viral load predicts progression
Positive confirms chronic infection; genotype guides therapy

sections.p: Liver injury in these settings follows a common sequence: viral replication or toxin exposure → hepatocyte apoptosis/necrosis → release of enzymes → inflammation and fibrosis.
b: Viral entry via hepatocyte receptors (HBV: NTCP, HCV: CD81)
Fibrogenesis via stellate cell activation → collagen deposition

sections.p: On imaging, liver size, texture and vascularity change with disease.
b: Cirrhosis – nodular surface, coarse echo pattern
Hepatocellular carcinoma – focal mass, arterial phase hyperenhancement

sections.p: Histology confirms the type of injury and stage of fibrosis.
b: Acute hepatitis – neutrophilic infiltrate, ballooning degeneration
Chronic hepatitis – lymphocytic infiltrate, interface hepatitis

sections.p: Symptoms vary with the underlying process but jaundice, abdominal pain and ascites are common.
b: Jaundice – yellowing of skin/eyes, pale stools
Right upper quadrant pain – hepatomegaly or cholangitis

sections.p: LFTs are the first step; further tests confirm etiology and severity.
b: Baseline LFTs – AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, bilirubin, albumin, INR
Viral load – HBV DNA, HCV RNA

t.b: High ALP with normal GGT suggests bone

sections.p: Severity is graded by enzyme levels and synthetic function; fibrosis is staged by biopsy or non‑invasive scores.
b: Acute liver failure – INR>1.5, encephalopathy, <7 days onset

sections.p: Complications drive mortality; early recognition improves outcomes.
b: Acute liver failure – fulminant death if untreated

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support liver function and prevent complications.
b: Antiviral therapy – tenofovir for HBV, DAAs for HCV
Supportive care – diuretics for ascites, lactulose for encephalopathy

sections.p: Lab patterns reflect underlying pathology and guide management.
b: Low albumin + high INR – synthetic failure

sections.p: History, exam, LFTs, imaging and serology form the diagnostic algorithm.
b: Ask about alcohol, drugs, travel, sexual history, family liver disease
Examine for jaundice, stigmata of chronic liver disease
Order baseline LFTs and viral serology
If acute liver failure, assess encephalopathy and INR

whenToSeekHelp: Acute jaundice with fever and abdominal pain (possible viral hepatitis or malaria), severe ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, sudden worsening of LFTs in a known liver disease patient

faq.q: Why is ALT more liver‑specific than AST?
faq.a: AST is also found in heart, muscle and red cells, so ALT rises mainly with hepatocyte injury.
Yes, severe falciparum malaria can cause hepatocellular injury, leading to mild to moderate transaminase elevations.

faq.q: When is a liver biopsy needed in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: When diagnosis remains uncertain after serology and imaging, or to stage fibrosis in chronic hepatitis B/C.

exam: 1. A 35‑year‑old man presents with jaundice and dark urine. LFTs show AST 80, ALT 90, ALP 120, GGT 110. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Viral hepatitis (HBV/HCV) – ALT/AST > ALP, GGT elevated.
2. A patient with chronic hepatitis B has ALT 120, AST 100, INR 1.4, albumin 3.8. What is the next step? — Start tenofovir; monitor LFTs and viral load.
3. A 28‑year‑old woman with fever, RUQ pain, LFTs AST 300, ALT 350, ALP 90. What is the most likely cause? — Acute viral hepatitis (viral or drug‑induced).
4. A patient on antitubercular therapy develops AST 400, ALT 450. What is the management? — Stop hepatotoxic drugs, give supportive care, consider alternative regimen.
5. A 50‑year‑old man with chronic alcohol use has AST 250, ALT 80. What does the AST/ALT ratio suggest? — Alcoholic hepatitis (ratio >2).
6. A patient with jaundice has normal ALP but high GGT. What does this indicate? — Biliary obstruction or cholestasis; GGT confirms biliary source.
7. A child presents with pale stools and abdominal pain. LFTs show ALP 200, GGT 180. What is the likely diagnosis? — Biliary atresia (or choledochal cyst).
8. A patient with cirrhosis develops sudden confusion and asterixis. What is the likely complication? — Hepatic encephalopathy; treat with lactulose.
9. A patient with chronic hepatitis B has a normal INR but low albumin. What does this suggest? — Early synthetic dysfunction; monitor closely.
10. A patient with acute malaria has LFTs AST 150, ALT 170. What is the significance? — Malaria can cause mild hepatocellular injury; monitor and treat malaria promptly.
11. A patient with elevated ALP and normal GGT is found to have a recent fracture. What explains the ALP rise? — Bone healing releases ALP; not liver disease.
12. A patient with chronic hepatitis C has normal ALT but high AST. What is the likely explanation? — Possible extra‑hepatic source (muscle) or lab error; repeat test.
